'''Arthur 'Blaine' Bowman''' (born 1946 in [[Ogden, Utah]], USA) is a leading proponent of [[ion chromatography]], who has served variously as chairman, president, chief executive officer, and director of [[Dionex Corporation]], a manufacturer of [[analytical instruments]]. Bowman received the 2015 [[Pittcon Heritage Award]] in recognition of his contributions to the field of ion chromatography.

== Early life and education ==
Arthur 'Blaine' Bowman was born in 1946 in [[Ogden, Utah]], US.<ref name=CHFBio>{{cite web|title=Pittcon Heritage Award: 2015 Winner A. Blaine Bowman|url=http://www.chemheritage.org/visit/events/awards/affiliate-partnership-awards/pittcon-heritage-award.aspx|website=Chemical Heritage Foundation|accessdate=30 July 2015|url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906004410/http://www.chemheritage.org/visit/events/awards/affiliate-partnership-awards/pittcon-heritage-award.aspx|archivedate=September 6, 2015}}</ref>  Around age 10, his family moved to Southern California, where he grew up.  Bowman attended [[Brigham Young University]] in [[Provo, Utah]] in the physics program. As an undergraduate, he worked in the summer as an engineer at [[McDonnell Douglas]], testing modules for the [[Apollo program|Apollo rocket]].<ref name=ACSInterview>{{cite journal|title=Business Page Executive Interview: A. Blaine Bowman, Dionex Corp.: I was looking for the opportunity to fulfill a dream|journal=Today's Chemist at Work|date=2003|volume=American Chemical Society|issue=April|page=35|url=http://pubs.acs.org/subscribe/archive/tcaw/12/i04/pdf/403business.pdf|accessdate=31 July 2015}}</ref> Bowman received his B.S. in physics in 1970.<ref name=CHFBio/>

Next, Bowman worked as a product engineer at [[Motorola]]'s [[Semiconductor]] Products Division in [[Phoenix, Arizona]], where he became interested in business. He attended [[Stanford University]]'s school of business from 1971 to 1973, receiving his M.B.A. in 1973.<ref name=ACSInterview/> He then joined [[McKinsey & Company]] as a [[management consultant]].<ref name=CHFBio/>

== Career ==
In 1977, Bowman joined International Plasma Corporation of [[Hayward, California]] as [[chief financial officer]] and general manager of its analytical instrument division.<ref name=CHFBio/> International Plasma Corporation owned Durrum Instrument Corporation, an instrumentation company that had purchased exclusive rights to an [[Emerging technologies|emergent technology]], [[Ion chromatography]], from [[Dow Chemical Company]]. Initial research by Hamish Small and others at the Dow Physical Research Laboratory in Midland, Michigan suggested that inorganic ion analysis would be superior to commonly used [[Wet chemistry|wet chemical techniques]], but Dow was not interested in pursuing the idea.<ref name=Business>{{cite web|title=Dionex Corporation - Company Profile, Information, Business Description, History, Background Information on Dionex Corporation|url=http://www.referenceforbusiness.com/history2/41/Dionex-Corporation.html|website=Reference for Business|accessdate=30 July 2015}}</ref><ref name=Stock>{{cite book|author-last=Small|author-first=Hamish|editor-last1=Stock|editor-first1=John T.|editor-last2=Orna|editor-first2=Mary Virginia|chapter=A personal history of the conception and early development of ion chromatography|title=The History and Preservation of Chemical Instrumentation, Proceedings of the ACS Division of the History of Chemistry Symposium held in Chicago, Ill., September 9-10, 1985|date=1986|publisher=Springer Netherlands|location=Dordrecht|isbn=978-9400946903}}</ref>

Bowman became interested in the potential of ion chromatography (IC) while at International Plasma Corporation.  In 1980, [[Smith-Kline]] acquired International Plasma Corporation.  The IC division was spun off as a separate company, under the name Dionex Corporation, in a [[leveraged buyout]] (LBO) led by A. Blaine Bowman.<ref name=Business/>  Bowman became the president and CEO of the new company, which was incorporated in California in 1980.<ref name=CHFBio/> The company was reincorporated in Delaware in 1986.<ref name=Annual2007>{{cite book|title=Annual Fund Report 2007|date=2007|publisher=Dionex Corporation|location=Sunnyvale, California|url=http://files.shareholder.com/downloads/DNEX/0x0x177241/EF519333-30F6-4046-881A-9EA35AFC22D0/Dio|access-date=2015-08-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304055417/http://files.shareholder.com/downloads/DNEX/0x0x177241/EF519333-30F6-4046-881A-9EA35AFC22D0/Dio|archive-date=2016-03-04|url-status=dead}}</ref>  Dionex began to trade publicly as of 1982.<ref name=WSJT/>

Under Bowman's leadership, Dionex made important advances both scientifically and economically. The company directed up to nine percent of its revenues back into its ongoing research and development program.  This enabled them to make a number of major technological improvements, including the introduction of fiber suppressors (1981), a metal-free system eliminating sources of contamination and corrosion (1981), integrated workstation and process analysis capabilities (1984), suppressors for gradient elution (1986) and [[accelerated solvent extraction]] (1995).<ref name=Business/> These technological changes made it possible for scientists to detect ionic materials quickly at extremely low levels of concentration.  This increased both the sensitivity of the tests that it was possible to do and the productivity of the people doing them. Bowman recognized the importance of developing software and data handling capabilities in support of Dionex's hardware.<ref name=WSJT/> Bowman has also emphasized the importance of marketing support, working closely with customers to ensure that they were satisfied with the products they were using, and developing new applications for customers' areas of interest.<ref name=Business/> He has stated that, in his opinion, what distinguished Dionex was that "we do provide a complete solutions approach for our customers. We don't just sell them hardware and walk away. We work with them to make sure that what we sell them makes them more effective and productive in their job."<ref name=WSJT/>

Through such improvements, Dionex was able to support much faster extraction of organic compounds for analysis from chemical mixtures, including complicated samples such as soils, polymers, and processed foods. The technology has wide application, in environmental testing laboratories, life science and food companies, chemical/petrochemical firms, power generation facilities, electronics manufacturers, government agencies, and academic institutions.<ref name=Bloomberg>{{cite web|title=Company Overview of Dionex Corp.|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/research/stocks/private/snapshot.asp?privcapId=27620|website=Bloomberg Business|accessdate=1 August 2015}}</ref> For example, during semiconductor production, Dionex instruments are used to detect and prevent ionic contamination, which can cause degradation of semiconductor surfaces and deterioration of their electrical properties.<ref name=Claeys>{{cite book|editor-last1=Claeys|editor-first1=C. L.|title=High purity silicon VI : proceedings of the Sixth International Symposium|date=2000|publisher=Electrochemical Society|location=Pennington, N.J.|isbn=9781566772846|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iGGr0SpJtaQC&pg=PA561|accessdate=1 August 2015}}</ref> The [[United States Environmental Protection Agency|Environmental Protection Agency]] has approved instruments such as the Dionex AS4 column for the analysis of anions in drinking water.<ref name=Business/> Dionex columns are used by municipalities seeking to ensure the safety of drinking water and by companies selling bottled waters.<ref name=DeBorba>{{cite web|last1=DeBorba|first1=Brian|last2=Rohrer|first2=Jeff|title=Determination of Trace Concentrations of Oxyhalides and Bromide in Municipal and Bottled Waters Using a Hydroxide- Selective Column with a Reagent-Free Ion Chromatography System|url=http://www.dionex.com/en-us/webdocs/10376-AN167-IC-Trace-Conc-Oxyhalides-Bromide-Municipal-AN70410_E.pdf|website=Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.|accessdate=1 August 2015}}</ref>

The company made a point of developing worldwide distribution channels:<ref name=Business/> as of 2007 Dionex's sales were distributed relatively evenly between North America, Europe, and the Asia/Pacific area.<ref name=Annual2007/> In the area of ion chromatography (IC), Dionex controlled more than 70 percent of a $200 million worldwide market.  In the newer area of [[high-performance liquid chromatography]] (HPLC), which Dionex entered in 1998, the company held a much smaller place (1%) in a much larger market ($2 billion market).<ref name=Business/><ref name=WSJT/>

Bowman directed the company from its early stages of development, as a small branch of a larger company with approximately $1 million in revenues in a year, to its position as publicly traded enterprise with an established international revenue stream in the hundreds of millions of dollars.<ref name=WSJT>{{cite journal|title=Blaine Bowman|journal= Wall Street Transcript Digest|date=September 30, 1999|url=http://www.twst.com/interview/3234|accessdate=30 July 2015}}</ref> Bowman retired as president and chief executive officer of Dionex in 2002.<ref name=Illumina/>  Net sales for fiscal 2002 were $182 million in spite of a shaky economic climate.<ref name=Annual2002>{{cite book|title=Dionex Corporation Annual 2002 Annual|date=2002|publisher=Dionex Corporation|location=Sunnyvale, California|url=http://files.shareholder.com/downloads/DNEX/0x0x56233/0330B1F0-9D79-42C3-9AA1-05982864B641/AR2002.pdf|access-date=2015-08-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304060340/http://files.shareholder.com/downloads/DNEX/0x0x56233/0330B1F0-9D79-42C3-9AA1-05982864B641/AR2002.pdf|archive-date=2016-03-04|url-status=dead}}</ref> Bowman retired as chairman of the board in 2005, but continued to serve on the board of directors.<ref name=Illumina/> Net sales for fiscal 2005 were $279.3 million,<ref name=Annual2005>{{cite book|title=Dionex Corporation 2005 Annual Report|date=2005|publisher=Dionex Corporation|location=Sunnyvale, California|url=http://globaldocuments.morningstar.com/documentlibrary/document/095f05faeea15bad.msdoc/original}} {{Dead link|date=October 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> and by 2007 had reached $327.3 million.<ref name=Annual2007/>

In 2010, Dionex was acquired by [[Thermo Fisher Scientific]] for $2.1 billion.<ref name=Rusli>{{cite news|last1=Rusli|first1=Evelyn M.|title=Thermo Fisher to Buy Lab Tool Maker|url=https://dealbook.nytimes.com/2010/12/13/thermo-fisher-buys-dionex-for-2-1-billion/?_r=0|accessdate=30 July 2015|work=The New York Times DealB%k|date=December 13, 2010}}</ref>

==Boards of Directors==
Bowman has served on the boards of directors of a number of companies in the areas of innovative technologies and the life sciences in addition to Dionex. From 1985 to 2007, Bowman served as a director of [[Molecular Devices|Molecular Devices Corporation]], a supplier of bioanalytical measurement instruments.<ref name=Illumina>{{cite web|title=Blaine Bowman|url=http://www.illumina.com/company/investor-information/corporate-governance/board-of-directors/blaine-bowman.html|website=Investor Information|publisher=Illumina|accessdate=30 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150730091809/http://www.illumina.com/company/investor-information/corporate-governance/board-of-directors/blaine-bowman.html|archive-date=30 July 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>  In 2006, he was appointed lead director of the board of Cell BioSciences, a [[privately held company]] engaged in protein research in the emerging area of nanoproteomics.<ref name=Biosciences>{{cite news|title=Cell Biosciences, Inc. Announces The Appointment Of Blaine Bowman As Lead Director|url=http://www.biospace.com/News/cell-biosciences-inc-announces-the-appointment-of/14058|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923190431/http://www.biospace.com/News/cell-biosciences-inc-announces-the-appointment-of/14058|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 23, 2015|accessdate=31 July 2015|work=BioSpace|date=March 31, 2006}}</ref><ref name=Nanoproteomics>{{cite journal|last1=Jia|first1=Lee|last2=Lu|first2=Yusheng|last3=Shao|first3=Jingwei|last4=Liang|first4=Xing-Jie|last5=Xu|first5=Yan|title=Nanoproteomics: a new sprout from emerging links between nanotechnology and proteomics|journal=Trends in Biotechnology|date=February 2013|volume=31|issue=2|pages=99–107|doi=10.1016/j.tibtech.2012.11.010|pmid=23280409}}</ref> He was appointed to the board of Solexa, Inc. in 2006.<ref name=Solexa>{{cite news|title=Solexa Appoints Blaine Bowman and Roy Whitfield to Board of Directors|url=http://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20060831005118/en/Solexa-Appoints-Blaine-Bowman-Roy-Whitfield-Board|accessdate=31 July 2015|work=BusinessWire|date=August 31, 2006}}</ref> Solexa, which developed genome sequencing technology, was acquired in 2007 by [[Illumina (company)|Illumina, Inc.]], on whose board of directors Bowman now serves. Illumina develops tools for DNA, RNA, and protein analysis.<ref name=Altera/> A. Blaine Bowman joined [[Altera Corporation]]'s board of directors as of July 30, 2012.<ref name=Altera>{{cite news|title=A. Blaine Bowman Joins Altera Board of Directors|url=https://www.altera.com/about/news_room/releases/_2012/corporate/nr-bowman.html|accessdate=30 July 2015|work=Altera Corporation Newsroom|date=July 30, 2012}}</ref> Altera develops [[programmable logic devices]].<ref name=Zacks13April2012>Zacks Equity Research, NASDAQ. "{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130129194232/http://community.nasdaq.com/News/2012-04/altera-shipping-28nm-fpgas-analyst-blog.aspx?storyid=133782|title=Altera Shipping 28-nm FPGAs}}." April 13, 2012. Retrieved May 8, 2012.</ref>

== Awards ==
Bowman was awarded the [[Pittcon Heritage Award]] in 2015,<ref name=Chromatography>{{cite journal|title=Chromatography Pioneer Scoops Prestigious Pittcon Award|journal=Chromatography Today|date=March 21, 2015|url=http://www.chromatographytoday.com/news/prep-chiral-green-gpc-ion/33/breaking_news/chromatography_pioneer_scoops_prestigious_pittcon_award/33877/|last1=Today |first1=Chromatography }}</ref><ref name="Pittcon">{{cite web|title=Pittcon Heritage Award|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/pittcon-heritage-award|website=[[Science History Institute]]|accessdate=23 March 2018|date=2016-05-31}}</ref> 
recognizing him for "providing the dedication, leadership and vision to commercialize ion chromatography and foster its evolution to a technology of critical importance for academic and a broad range of industries."<ref name=Taylor>{{cite journal|last1=Taylor|first1=Michelle|title=Pittcon Award Honors Ion Chrom Pioneer|journal=Laboratory Equipment|date=March 9, 2015|url=http://www.laboratoryequipment.com/articles/2015/03/pittcon-award-honors-ion-chrom-pioneer|accessdate=31 July 2015}}</ref>
